 WASHINGTON (TNND) — With days left before Election Day, Iowa’s open U.S. Senate race is emerging as one of the country's tightest contests, with Republican U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson and Democrat Josh Turek locked in a toss-up. Recent polling averages show the contest as essentially even, with Hinson ahead by less than a point, in a race that could help decide which party controls the Senate.
 In an interview on the National News Desk, Hinson said her campaign is centered on lowering costs and described herself as “the common sense minivan driving mom, trying to drive that common sense back into Washington, DC.” (TNND)
 Voters in Iowa, as in other parts of the country, are focused on affordability, high gas and diesel prices, agriculture and rural health care.
 In an interview on the National News Desk, Hinson said her campaign is centered on lowering costs and described herself as “the common sense minivan driving mom, trying to drive that common sense back into Washington, DC.”
 Hinson said her priorities include making “the working families tax cuts” permanent, along with “no tax on tips, no tax on overtime and no tax on Social Security.”
 On fuel prices, Hinson said Iowa should embrace biofuels, including E15, which she described as ethanol in fuel. She said E15 is “a great consumer choice that on average is about 30 cents a gallon cheaper,” and said she would like to see it available nationwide year-round. She also pointed to biodiesel production in Iowa as a way to help drive down prices.
 On housing, Hinson said the average age of a first-time homebuyer is now over 40. She said she has legislation that would use a tax-deferred savings mechanism similar to a 529 model to help people save for their first home.
 Asked about high gas and diesel prices and international conflict, Hinson said, “We need to bring the war to an immediate and successful end.” She also said the U.S. should focus on long-term energy certainty by investing in domestic refining capacity and reducing reliance on foreign energy sources. Hinson said the country should avoid “sending signals to these producers” that federal policy will change abruptly, and she pointed to supply chain investments, including steel production tied to mining in Minnesota and manufacturing in Iowa.
 On rural hospitals and maternity care access, Hinson said she supported more than $50 billion in funding and said $200 million “has already been deployed here in Iowa.” She said the money is being used to recruit providers and purchase equipment, citing examples that included hiring a physician’s assistant and nurse midwife, buying a new MRI machine, and purchasing a lung cancer detection machine.
 Hinson criticized her opponent, saying, “My opponent in this race Josh Turek couldn’t even be bothered to show up for the vote on this funding.” She also said Turek “skipped 58 percent of his votes at the state capital this year.”
 The interview also touched on reports about President Donald Trump’s campaign schedule. Hinson said she had not spoken with Trump that day but said she would welcome him back to Iowa. “If the president comes Sunday, I’ll be there,” she said. Otherwise, she said she would continue campaigning between now and November 3rd.
 Hinson also attacked Turek on immigration, saying, “It’s a choice between common sense and crazy,” and claiming her opponent supports “those immigration open border policies.” She said Turek “voted to allow taxpayer benefits to go to illegals and to make it easier for sanctuary city sheriffs to avoid working with immigration enforcement.”
